item.text: {"question_id":"4B.7","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi’s government enacted or maintained several formal protections relevant to excluded groups: the Indigenous Peoples’ rights law, a victim-reparation framework providing legal assistance, protection, health care, compensation, and guarantees of non-repetition, and laws and programs addressing gender-based violence, disability, and reproductive health. The 2023 elections also extended voting to citizens abroad, had broad party-candidate registration, and included citizen observers. These measures show formal and partial institutional inclusion, but they do not establish equal enforcement or access. Election registration and voter education under-reached women, Indigenous people, persons with disabilities, and internally displaced people; polling infrastructure was inaccessible; women won only 61 of 477 initially confirmed National Assembly seats; and voting did not occur in conflict-affected territories. Persistent gender disparities, girls’ exclusion from education, conflict-related displacement and school closures, discrimination against Indigenous peoples and persons with disabilities, and discrimination and violence against LGBTQI+ people further demonstrate unequal practical access. The government’s own reported reforms and some regulatory responses provide positive evidence, but implementation was generally ineffective or incomplete, services and remedies remained constrained, and most outcomes cannot be attributed personally to Tshisekedi. Conflict and armed-group control materially qualify attribution for some regional exclusions, while aligned-official ethnic-regional rhetoric adversely affected the political environment without supplied evidence that Tshisekedi authored or endorsed
